# Gaṅgamālajātaka (Ja 421)
**ID:** Ja 421
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Gaṅgamālajātaka* (Ja 421) is a canonical Jātaka tale set during the Buddha's stay at Jetavana, delivered to lay followers regarding the benefits and conduct appropriate to observing the weekly holy days (*uposatha*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The narrative recounts how King Udaya of Benares achieved royal splendour as the karmic fruit of partially observing a holy day in a previous life [SuttaCentral; Cowell 1897; Jones 1956]. The king repeatedly recites an enigmatic utterance (*udānagāthā*) that puzzles his court [Cowell 1897]. Prompted by the chief queen, the royal barber Gaṅgamāla uses tweezers before his razor to induce the king into granting a boon, thereby discovering the meaning of the king's verse and his former life of poverty [Cowell 1897; Fausböll 1883]. Emulating the renunciation of worldly desires rather than yielding to craving for wealth or status, Gaṅgamāla retires to the Himālayas, attains paccekabuddhahood, and later flies through the air to visit King Udaya, whom he addresses as Brahmadatta [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897; Fenn 1994; Hahn et al. 1997]. Epigraphic and temple records demonstrate that the story was illustrated and identified under variant spellings (such as *Gangamāla*, *Kaikamāla*, and *Phaṅkamāla*) in Pagan period temples in Burma [WinThanTun 2002].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral identify a full Sanskrit parallel in the *Mahāvastu* (Mvu 84, *The Jātaka of Gaṅgapāla*), and the text is cited in the *Mahāniddesa* (Mnd 1, Mnd 2) and *Cullaniddesa* (Cnd 5) [SuttaCentral]. This alignment is substantiated by DharmaNexus, which computes 13 cross-language matches between Ja 421 and the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu-avadāna* [DharmaNexus]. Text-critical studies further highlight close verse and phrase parallels between the Pali Jātaka, the *Mahāvastu*, and the *Saṅghabhedavastu* [Jones 1956; Marciniak 2019]. Within Pali literature, DharmaNexus detects 14 matching passages shared between the canonical verses and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
